performers: Reinald Werrenrath, baritone; Mabel Garrison, soprano; orchestra conducted by Josef Pasternack
intro: Don Giovanni persuades Zerlina one phrase at a time, until the two voices are dancing together in 6/8. Reinald Werrenrath and Mabel Garrison sing Mozart’s little duet on this 1920 Victor recording, with Josef Pasternack conducting.

sections.label: A · Giovanni invites, Zerlina hesitates
sections.mNote: Separate voices in the A-major Andante

sections.label: A′ · Shorter replies, wavering answer
sections.mNote: Giovanni repeats his offer between Zerlina’s replies

sections.label: B · Andiam, in 6/8
sections.mNote: Both voices sing together in the quicker dance

cues.title: Giovanni makes his offer
cues.text: Giovanni has got Zerlina’s bridegroom out of the way. He offers her an easy A-major tune and the promise of a new life. The strings play quiet chords between the bass notes, leaving plenty of room for his voice.
cues.evidence: Schirmer Italian–English vocal score, plate 15147, No. 7, p. 64: Andante, A major, quiet string accompaniment. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/1a/IMSLP68957-PMLP36804-Mozart_-_Don_Giovanni_it-eng_Vocal_Score.pdf. The preceding scene sends Masetto away: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Là_ci_darem_la_mano
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Zerlina weighs the offer
cues.text: Zerlina answers in the same gentle A major. Her words hesitate: “I would like to, and I wouldn’t.” Her heart trembles; she thinks of Masetto and fears Giovanni may deceive her.
cues.evidence: Da Ponte’s libretto for Don Giovanni (1787), Act I, No. 7; Zerlina’s Vorrei e non vorrei, translated here. Schirmer vocal score, pp. 64–65. Italian text: https://www.opera-arias.com/mozart/don-giovanni/la-ci-darem-la-mano/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Camden, February 1920
cues.text: Mabel Garrison and Reinald Werrenrath record the duet in Camden, New Jersey, on 18 February 1920. Josef Pasternack conducts. Their performance fits on a ten-inch Victor disc, catalogue number 87569.
cues.evidence: Library of Congress National Jukebox catalogue, recording date, Camden location, performers, conductor and ten-inch Victor 87569: https://www.loc.gov/item/jukebox-35668/

cues.title: Two voices, one dance
cues.text: The closing Allegro changes from 2/4 to 6/8. Giovanni and Zerlina sing together, much of the time a third apart, with the same words on their lips: “Andiam” — let us go.
cues.evidence: Schirmer vocal score, pp. 66–67: the fermata before Allegro, the change to 6/8 and the voices in parallel thirds. Da Ponte’s Andiam is translated here.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Elvira interrupts the lovers
cues.text: In the opera, Donna Elvira interrupts the couple as soon as the duet ends. “Stop, wretch!” she calls to Giovanni, and takes Zerlina away.
cues.evidence: Da Ponte’s Don Giovanni libretto (1787), recitative following No. 7; Fermati, scellerato! translated here. Schirmer vocal score, p. 68; the action is summarised at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Là_ci_darem_la_mano

transitions.title: The invitation comes in fragments
transitions.how: The A-major invitation returns in shorter phrases. Giovanni restarts his offer between Zerlina’s replies; the bass keeps short pulses beneath quiet string chords. Her chromatic descent on “Non son più forte” — I can resist no longer — draws the exchange towards its pause.
transitions.evidence: Schirmer vocal score, plate 15147, pp. 65–66: the shortened exchanges and Zerlina’s descending chromatic line before Andiam. Translation here is our own.

transitions.title: A pause, then the shared dance
transitions.how: After Zerlina’s assent, a fermata holds the music still. The Andante in 2/4 becomes an Allegro in 6/8. A major stays in place; held bass notes support the lilting accompaniment, and the two singers move together in parallel thirds.
transitions.evidence: Schirmer vocal score, plate 15147, pp. 66–67: fermata, Allegro, 6/8 and the joint vocal phrases over held bass notes.

composer.epithet: In his operas a servant can outwit a count; in his concertos the piano can interrupt before the orchestra has finished its opening sentence.
facts: He usually called himself Wolfgang Amadè Mozart
Childhood tours across Europe; three Italian visits, 1769–73
His home from 1781; concertos, quartets and the Da Ponte operas

quote.text: In an opera, poetry must simply be music’s obedient daughter.
quote.source: Mozart to his father Leopold, Vienna, 13 October 1781; our translation

composer.background:
When Leopold Mozart arrived in Vienna on 11 February 1785, the copyist was still writing out his son’s new concerto for that evening’s concert at the Mehlgrube. Wolfgang had been so busy supervising the copying that he had found no time to try the finale through. This was K. 466 in D minor: restless, syncopated strings, then a piano entering with a tune of its own. Leopold thought the concert splendid.

The next day, Haydn heard three quartets at Wolfgang’s home. Leopold recorded his verdict in a letter to Nannerl begun on 14 February: “Before God, and as an honest man, I tell you that your son is the greatest composer I know, personally or by name.” Haydn praised his taste and his knowledge of composition. Mozart would dedicate the quartets to him.
